claim: 72 PVALB-enriched genes have conserved expression patterns in both human medial temporal gyrus (MTG) and mouse primary visual cortex (VISp).
source: We identified 72 PVALB- and 75 SST-enriched genes whose expression patterns were conserved in both human medial temporal gyrus (MTG) and mouse primary visual cortex (VISp; Tasic et al., 2018; Hodge et al., 2019; Figure 1a, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic analysis data comparing human and mouse cortex, as shown in Figure 1a and Supplementary file 1, and cites published references.

claim: 75 SST-enriched genes have conserved expression patterns in both human medial temporal gyrus (MTG) and mouse primary visual cortex (VISp).
source: We identified 72 PVALB- and 75 SST-enriched genes whose expression patterns were conserved in both human medial temporal gyrus (MTG) and mouse primary visual cortex (VISp; Tasic et al., 2018; Hodge et al., 2019; Figure 1a, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic analysis data comparing human and mouse cortex, as shown in Figure 1a and Supplementary file 1, and cites published references.

claim: Gene expression patterns of PVALB- and SST-enriched genes are similar in primary motor cortex (M1 in human, MOp in mouse).
source: These patterns were similar in primary motor cortex (M1 in human, MOp in mouse), consistent with reports of similar transcriptomic GABAergic neuron type properties across mouse cortical areas (Tasic et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic data analysis and cites a published reference.

claim: The most significantly enriched Gene Ontology terms for conserved genes between PVALB and SST neurons are synapse-related categories.
source: The most significantly enriched GO terms were for synapse related categories, with postsynaptic membrane Gene Ontology term GO:0045211 (http://www.informatics.jax.org/vocab/gene_ontology/GO:0045211) being enriched in both PVALB and SST neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by Gene Ontology analysis results shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Postsynaptic membrane Gene Ontology term GO:0045211 is enriched in both PVALB and SST neurons.
source: The most significantly enriched GO terms were for synapse related categories, with postsynaptic membrane Gene Ontology term GO:0045211 (http://www.informatics.jax.org/vocab/gene_ontology/GO:0045211) being enriched in both PVALB and SST neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by Gene Ontology analysis results.

claim: Many conserved genes that discriminate between PVALB and SST subclass cells are involved in regulating synaptic connectivity and their functional properties.
source: This suggests that many of the conserved genes that discriminate between PVALB and SST subclass cells are involved in regulating synaptic connectivity and their functional properties.
evidence: The claim is inferred from Gene Ontology analysis showing enrichment of synapse-related categories.

claim: Elfn1 gene is enriched in GABAergic interneurons compared to excitatory neurons.
source: Among these, the Elfn1 gene, described to mediate selective short-term facilitation in SST interneurons (Sylwestrak and Ghosh, 2012; de Wit and Ghosh, 2016; Stachniak et al., 2019), is enriched in GABAergic interneurons compared to excitatory neurons, and in SST and all other GABAergic subclasses except PVALB interneurons, we found that this pattern is conserved across both species and cortical areas (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic data shown in Figure 1c and cites published references.

claim: Elfn1 is enriched in SST and all other GABAergic subclasses except PVALB interneurons.
source: Among these, the Elfn1 gene, described to mediate selective short-term facilitation in SST interneurons (Sylwestrak and Ghosh, 2012; de Wit and Ghosh, 2016; Stachniak et al., 2019), is enriched in GABAergic interneurons compared to excitatory neurons, and in SST and all other GABAergic subclasses except PVALB interneurons, we found that this pattern is conserved across both species and cortical areas (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic data shown in Figure 1c and cites published references.

claim: The expression pattern of Elfn1 in GABAergic subclasses is conserved across both species and cortical areas.
source: Among these, the Elfn1 gene, described to mediate selective short-term facilitation in SST interneurons (Sylwestrak and Ghosh, 2012; de Wit and Ghosh, 2016; Stachniak et al., 2019), is enriched in GABAergic interneurons compared to excitatory neurons, and in SST and all other GABAergic subclasses except PVALB interneurons, we found that this pattern is conserved across both species and cortical areas (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic data shown in Figure 1c comparing human and mouse cortex.

claim: There are molecular substrates for conserved synaptic properties that differentiate PVALB and SST subclass interneurons.
source: Together, these analyses suggest there are molecular substrates for conserved synaptic properties that differentiate PVALB and SST subclass interneurons (Blackman et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is inferred from transcriptomic analysis showing differential gene expression and cites a published reference.

source: In acute slice preparations, neurons were targeted based on somatic shape as visualized by oblique illumination.

claim: In slice culture experiments, AAV vectors were used to transduce GABAergic neurons and drive expression of fluorescent reporters under the control of cell-class-selective regulatory elements.
source: In slice culture experiments, AAV vectors were used to transduce GABAergic neurons and drive expression of fluorescent reporters under the control of cell-class-selective regulatory elements to facilitate targeting labeled neurons for multiple patch-clamp recordings (Schwarz et al., 2019; Mich et al., 2021).

claim: The use of reporter AAV vectors has not been seen to significantly impact the physiology or morphology of cortical neurons.
source: The use of reporter AAV vectors can greatly facilitate prospective marking of GABAergic cells, and has not been seen to significantly impact the physiology or morphology of cortical neurons (Lee et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and cites a published reference.

claim: Two strategies were used to identify GABAergic subclass identity: mFISH analysis with subclass markers and a machine learning classifier based on Patch-seq analysis.
source: After multiple patch-clamp electrophysiology experiments, two strategies were used to identify GABAergic subclass identity, including an mFISH analysis with subclass markers and a machine learning classifier based on Patch-seq analysis using similar human slice preparations.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the manuscript describing the experimental approach.

claim: Individual presynaptic pyramidal neurons evoke postsynaptic responses with heterogeneous synaptic dynamics in different postsynaptic cell types.
source: We find that there are robust molecular differences in synapse-associated genes between these neuron types, and that individual presynaptic pyramidal neurons evoke postsynaptic responses with heterogeneous synaptic dynamics in different postsynaptic cell types.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: PVALB neurons typically show depressing synaptic characteristics.
source: Using molecular identification with FISH and classifiers based on transcriptomically identified PVALB neurons analyzed by Patch-seq, we find that PVALB neurons typically show depressing synaptic characteristics, whereas other interneuron types including SST-positive neurons show facilitating characteristics.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Other interneuron types including SST-positive neurons show facilitating synaptic characteristics.
source: Using molecular identification with FISH and classifiers based on transcriptomically identified PVALB neurons analyzed by Patch-seq, we find that PVALB neurons typically show depressing synaptic characteristics, whereas other interneuron types including SST-positive neurons show facilitating characteristics.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Target cell-specific synaptic properties exist in human cortex that are similar to rodent.
source: Together, these data support the existence of target cell-specific synaptic properties in human cortex that are similar to rodent, thereby indicating evolutionary conservation of local circuit connectivity motifs from excitatory to inhibitory neurons and their synaptic dynamics.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: There is evolutionary conservation of local circuit connectivity motifs from excitatory to inhibitory neurons and their synaptic dynamics.
source: Together, these data support the existence of target cell-specific synaptic properties in human cortex that are similar to rodent, thereby indicating evolutionary conservation of local circuit connectivity motifs from excitatory to inhibitory neurons and their synaptic dynamics.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of human and rodent data presented in the manuscript.

claim: When two pyramidal neurons were connected to the same postsynaptic inhibitory neuron, they typically showed similar kinetics of short-term synaptic plasticity.
source: As shown in Figure 4b and c, when two pyramidal neurons were connected to the same postsynaptic inhibitory neuron, they typically showed similar kinetics of short-term synaptic plasticity that was either depressing or facilitating depending on the postsynaptic neuron.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b and c.

claim: When one presynaptic pyramidal neuron was connected to 2 interneurons, the short-term synaptic plasticity was often different for the two interneurons.
source: Similarly, when one presynaptic pyramidal neuron was connected to 2 interneurons, the short-term synaptic plasticity was often different for the two interneurons (Figure 4d).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Postsynaptic cell identity is a determinant of short-term synaptic dynamics in excitatory to inhibitory neuron connections in human cortex.
source: Both results indicate that postsynaptic cell identity is a determinant of short-term synaptic dynamics (i.e. target cell-specific) in excitatory to inhibitory neuron connections in human cortex (Reyes et al., 1998; Markram et al., 1998; Koester and Johnston, 2005).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4, and cites published references.

claim: Target-dependent synaptic properties were observed in both acute and slice culture preparations.
source: These target-dependent synaptic properties were observed in both acute and slice culture preparations (Figure 4b–d).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: 50 Hz stimulation protocol showed stronger depression with bigger EPSP responses compared to the 20 Hz stimulation protocol.
source: Here, 50 Hz stimulation protocol showed stronger depression with bigger EPSP responses (upper heatmap in both acute and slice culture data, Figure 4e and f) compared to the 20 Hz stimulation protocol (Figure 4g and h).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4e-h.

claim: Amounts of depression are dependent on presynaptic stimulus frequencies.
source: These results show that amounts of depression are dependent on presynaptic stimulus frequencies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a and b).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a and b.

claim: Depressing synapses had higher EPSP amplitudes than facilitating synapses.
source: However, the depressing synapses had higher EPSP amplitudes than facilitating synapses (Figure 4j, left panel; Linear regression between PPR and EPSP amplitude, R-squared=0.079452, p=0.0074488), and this difference was not accounted for by disease indication or slice preparation method (p=0.00029819 for depression/facilitation, p=0.7852 for epilepsy/tumor, p=0.2766 for acute/culture, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4j with statistical analysis.

claim: There was a significant correlation between the degree of facilitation/depression (PPR) and recovery rate in early time periods within 250ms.
source: When we parameterized the degree of facilitation/depression (i.e. PPR) and recovery rate in early time periods within 250ms, there was a significant correlation between these parameters (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) that showed distinct synaptic recovery dynamics between the two synapse types.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Recovery responses were not accounted for by disease indication or slice preparation method.
source: Their recovery responses (i.e. 9th pulse at various time intervals) were also not accounted for by disease indication (p=0.4781) or slice preparation method (p=0.7816, two-way ANOVA with repeated measures as different recovery time periods).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Normalized synaptic dynamics were not impacted by disease state of the donor or slice preparation method.
source: Similarly, normalized synaptic dynamics (i.e. normalized responses from first to 8th pulses at both 20 Hz and 50 Hz; Figure 4—figure supplement 1c) were not impacted by disease state of the donor, or slice preparation method with two-way ANOVA with repeated measures (both p>0.05).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: More facilitating synapses were detected in slice cultures than in acute slices.
source: Indeed, more facilitating synapses were detected in slice cultures than in acute slices. Based on the train-induced STP (1:6–8 ratio), about 30% of recordings (n=17) in slice cultures (total n=56) showed facilitation, compared to only 12% of recordings (n=4) in acute slices (total n=33; Figure 4f and h).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4f and h.

claim: About 30% of recordings (n=17) in slice cultures (total n=56) showed facilitation based on the train-induced STP (1:6–8 ratio).
source: Based on the train-induced STP (1:6–8 ratio), about 30% of recordings (n=17) in slice cultures (total n=56) showed facilitation, compared to only 12% of recordings (n=4) in acute slices (total n=33; Figure 4f and h).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data.

claim: Only 12% of recordings (n=4) in acute slices (total n=33) showed facilitation based on the train-induced STP (1:6–8 ratio).
source: Based on the train-induced STP (1:6–8 ratio), about 30% of recordings (n=17) in slice cultures (total n=56) showed facilitation, compared to only 12% of recordings (n=4) in acute slices (total n=33; Figure 4f and h).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data.

claim: There was no significant correlation between PPR change and days in slice culture.
source: To address the potential changes of short-term synaptic dynamics by increasing spontaneous synaptic activity that has been previously observed during slice culture (Napoli and Obeid, 2016), we analyzed the PPR change as a function of days in slice culture and did not observe a significant correlation (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4, and cites a published reference.

claim: Initial EPSP amplitudes in the pairs with postsynaptic PVALB-positive neurons were larger compared to those of postsynaptic SST-positive neurons.
source: Initial EPSP amplitudes in the pairs with postsynaptic PVALB-positive neurons were larger compared to those of postsynaptic SST-positive neurons (EPSP amplitudes, mean ± s.e.m, 4.7393±1.3975 mV with PVALB-positive postsynaptic neuron, 0.8412±0.3147 mV with SST-positive postsynaptic neuron, p=0.0159, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Synaptic dynamics with PVALB-positive neurons showed strong depression.
source: Whereas synaptic dynamics with PVALB-positive neurons showed strong depression, synaptic dynamics with SST-positive neurons showed facilitation and their normalized trained responses were different (i.e. 2–8 pulse responses in Figure 5f; *, p<0.05, Wilcoxon rank sum test, n=5 for PVALB and n=6 for SST neurons).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5f with statistical analysis.

claim: Synaptic dynamics with SST-positive neurons showed facilitation.
source: Whereas synaptic dynamics with PVALB-positive neurons showed strong depression, synaptic dynamics with SST-positive neurons showed facilitation and their normalized trained responses were different (i.e. 2–8 pulse responses in Figure 5f; *, p<0.05, Wilcoxon rank sum test, n=5 for PVALB and n=6 for SST neurons).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5f with statistical analysis.

claim: Normalized trained responses were different between PVALB-positive and SST-positive neurons (2–8 pulse responses, p<0.05).
source: Whereas synaptic dynamics with PVALB-positive neurons showed strong depression, synaptic dynamics with SST-positive neurons showed facilitation and their normalized trained responses were different (i.e. 2–8 pulse responses in Figure 5f; *, p<0.05, Wilcoxon rank sum test, n=5 for PVALB and n=6 for SST neurons).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5f with statistical analysis.

claim: A classifier trained on intrinsic features from Patch-seq neurons predicted PVALB subclass identity with 76% accuracy.
source: A classifier trained on these intrinsic features from Patch-seq neurons predicted PVALB subclass identity with 76% accuracy (cross-validated prediction, with 29% false positive rate, 14% false negative rate).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by machine learning analysis of experimental data.

claim: The classifier for PVALB subclass identity had a 29% false positive rate and 14% false negative rate.
source: A classifier trained on these intrinsic features from Patch-seq neurons predicted PVALB subclass identity with 76% accuracy (cross-validated prediction, with 29% false positive rate, 14% false negative rate).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by machine learning analysis of experimental data.

claim: Cells with positive PVALB labeling had high PVALB prediction probabilities.
source: Importantly, quantitative predictions for the PVALB identity of postsynaptic interneurons from multiple patch-clamp recordings also matched well with mFISH labeling for those cells. Specifically, cells with positive PVALB labeling had high PVALB prediction probabilities, whereas cells with positive SST or VIP labeling had low PVALB prediction probabilities (Figure 6b).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Cells with positive SST or VIP labeling had low PVALB prediction probabilities.
source: Importantly, quantitative predictions for the PVALB identity of postsynaptic interneurons from multiple patch-clamp recordings also matched well with mFISH labeling for those cells. Specifically, cells with positive PVALB labeling had high PVALB prediction probabilities, whereas cells with positive SST or VIP labeling had low PVALB prediction probabilities (Figure 6b).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: The features with highest weighting in the classifier were AP height, depolarizing sag, AP upstroke adaptation ratio, and membrane time constant.
source: The features with highest weighting in the classifier were AP height, depolarizing sag, AP upstroke adaptation ratio, and membrane time constant (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by machine learning analysis shown in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Cells with a high likelihood of being PVALB-positive tended to show synaptic depression as shown by the correlation between paired pulse ratios and PVALB probability using 50 Hz pulse trains.
source: As expected, cells with a high likelihood of being PVALB-positive tended to show synaptic depression as shown by the correlation between paired pulse ratios and PVALB probability using 50 Hz pulse trains.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6e.

claim: Paired pulse ratio is a better metric (p=0.0092262) to predict PVALB type compared to EPSP amplitude (p=0.079456).
source: This result shows that paired pulse ratio is better metric (p=0.0092262) to predict PVALB type compared to EPSP amplitude (P=0.079456) (see also Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There is correlation between EPSP amplitudes and paired pulse ratios especially in non-PVALB type.
source: In addition, we looked at the relationship between EPSP amplitudes and paired pulse ratios within each type (i.e. PVALB vs non-PVALB) to see whether EPSP amplitudes have separable effects on short-term dynamics (Figure 6—figure supplement 2). The outcome shows that there is correlation between EPSP amplitudes and paired pulse ratios especially in non-PVALB type, indicating that EPSP amplitudes and short-term dynamics may be related in a subclass cell-type specific manner.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: EPSP amplitudes and short-term dynamics may be related in a subclass cell-type specific manner.
source: The outcome shows that there is correlation between EPSP amplitudes and paired pulse ratios especially in non-PVALB type, indicating that EPSP amplitudes and short-term dynamics may be related in a subclass cell-type specific manner.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Target cell-dependent principles and specific properties of synaptic plasticity in PVALB versus other interneuron types appear to be strongly conserved between human and rodent.
source: Therefore, both the target cell-dependent principles and the specific properties of synaptic plasticity in PVALB versus other interneuron types appear to be strongly conserved, suggesting similar roles in functional cortical circuitry across species.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and inferred from the comparison of human and rodent data throughout the manuscript.

claim: PVALB-positive basket-like cells in human cortex are very likely to have similar functional roles in cortical circuits as in rodents.
source: Given the conserved intrinsic properties of human and rodent PVALB neurons (i.e. fast spiking) and their target-specific depressing synaptic dynamics, PVALB-positive basket-like cells in human cortex are very likely to have similar functional roles in cortical circuits.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the conserved properties observed in the experimental data.

claim: PVALB neurons likely mediate excitation-inhibition balance, gain control, and generation/synchronization of fast oscillation in the gamma frequency range (20–80 Hz).
source: These roles likely include mediation of excitation-inhibition balance, gain control, and generation/synchronization of fast oscillation (e.g. 'gamma' frequency range, 20–80 Hz) by communicating with reciprocally connected neighboring excitatory neurons (Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011).
evidence: The claim is inferred from established knowledge and cites a published reference.

claim: Non-PVALB interneurons, including SST-stained neurons, showed rather small initial EPSP responses and tended to have short-term synaptic facilitation.
source: Non-PVALB interneurons, including SST-stained neurons by post-hoc HCR, instead showed rather small initial EPSP responses and tended to have short-term synaptic facilitation.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by experimental data.

claim: Putative 'Martinotti' cells in human cortex contribute to lateral disynaptic inhibition between two neighboring pyramidal neurons via receiving delayed facilitating synapses.
source: Putative 'Martinotti' cells in human cortex also contribute to lateral disynaptic inhibition between two neighboring pyramidal neurons via receiving delayed facilitating synapses (Obermayer et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and cites a published reference.

claim: ELFN1 is expressed in all interneuron subclasses except PVALB neurons, and this pattern is conserved from mouse to human.
source: We find that ELFN1 is expressed in all interneuron subclasses except PVALB neurons, and this pattern is conserved from mouse to human, suggesting a similar role in non-PVALB expressing interneurons from mouse to human (Jorstad et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by transcriptomic data, and cites a published reference.

claim: ELFN1 expression pattern suggests a similar role in non-PVALB expressing interneurons from mouse to human.
source: We find that ELFN1 is expressed in all interneuron subclasses except PVALB neurons, and this pattern is conserved from mouse to human, suggesting a similar role in non-PVALB expressing interneurons from mouse to human (Jorstad et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the conserved expression pattern and cites a published reference.

claim: Human cortex shows faster recovery from synaptic depression compared to rodents.
source: These studies have demonstrated many conserved features, but also a variety of human specializations compared to rodents including faster recovery from synaptic depression (Testa-Silva et al., 2014) and greater numbers of functional release sites (Szegedi et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and cites published references.

claim: Human cortex has greater numbers of functional release sites compared to rodents.
source: These studies have demonstrated many conserved features, but also a variety of human specializations compared to rodents including faster recovery from synaptic depression (Testa-Silva et al., 2014) and greater numbers of functional release sites (Szegedi et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and cites published references.

claim: Elfn1 mediates selective short-term facilitation in SST interneurons.
source: Among these, the Elfn1 gene, described to mediate selective short-term facilitation in SST interneurons (Sylwestrak and Ghosh, 2012; de Wit and Ghosh, 2016; Stachniak et al., 2019), is enriched in GABAergic interneurons compared to excitatory neurons, and in SST and all other GABAergic subclasses except PVALB interneurons, we found that this pattern is conserved across both species and cortical areas (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and cites published references.

claim: Specialized short-term facilitation in SST interneurons is mediated by Elfn1 expression in postsynaptic dendritic shafts of SST cells.
source: This specialized short-term facilitation in SST interneurons is known to be mediated by Elfn1 expression in postsynaptic dendritic shafts of SST cells (Sylwestrak and Ghosh, 2012; de Wit and Ghosh, 2016; Stachniak et al., 2019), but not in PVALB neurons.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and cites published references.

claim: Elfn1 in postsynaptic SST neurons interacts with presynaptic metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs) and kainate receptors in a layer-specific manner.
source: This molecular mechanism was originally discovered in the hippocampus but was extended to the cerebral cortex showing that Elfn1 in postsynaptic SST neurons interacts with presynaptic metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs) and kainate receptors in a layer-specific manner (Stachniak et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and cites a published reference.

claim: 45 types of inhibitory interneurons have been reported in mouse and human cortex that can be discriminated using genome-wide gene expression.
source: Advances in single cell transcriptomics have demonstrated a highly complex cellular architecture in the mouse and human cortex, with 45 types of inhibitory interneurons reported that can be discriminated using genome-wide gene expression (Hodge et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and cites a published reference.

claim: PVALB and SST neurons correspond to major divisions among GABAergic interneurons at the subclass level.
source: PVALB and SST neurons correspond to major divisions among GABAergic interneurons at the subclass level, along with LAMP5 and VIP subclasses.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and based on established transcriptomic classification.

claim: Comparative transcriptomic analyses show a generally conserved cell type organization from mouse to human.
source: Comparative transcriptomic analyses show a generally conserved cell type organization from mouse to human, but with many changes in cellular gene expression that suggest differences in cellular physiology, anatomy, and connectivity (Hodge et al., 2019; Bakken et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and cites published references.

claim: There are many changes in cellular gene expression from mouse to human that suggest differences in cellular physiology, anatomy, and connectivity.
source: Comparative transcriptomic analyses show a generally conserved cell type organization from mouse to human, but with many changes in cellular gene expression that suggest differences in cellular physiology, anatomy, and connectivity (Hodge et al., 2019; Bakken et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and cites published references.

claim: The same functional readouts could be achieved through distinct molecular mechanisms across species.
source: Whether these species differences lead to functional differences has been a topic of great debate, as it is well known that the same functional readouts, such as synaptic connectivity and dynamics, could be achieved through distinct molecular mechanisms across species (Goaillard and Marder, 2021).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and cites a published reference.

claim: Electrophysiological properties and local synaptic connectivity can be studied in acute human neocortical slices derived from surgical resections.
source: Recent work has shown that electrophysiological properties and local synaptic connectivity can be studied in acute human neocortical slices derived from surgical resections (Molnár et al., 2008; Jiang et al., 2012; Testa-Silva et al., 2014; Kalmbach et al., 2018; Beaulieu-Laroche et al., 2018; Boldog et al., 2018; Seeman et al., 2018; Peng et al., 2019; Planert et al., 2021; Campagnola et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and cites multiple published references.

claim: Conservation of cellular properties between human and model organisms is often seen but cannot be assumed.
